# DGXX: Behind-the-meter power for AI data centers as grid capex flatlines

## Bear case first
The 10-Q names Cerebras and warns that the company's ability to continue as a going concern depends on obtaining significant funding [16]. Colocation revenue fell from $9.6M to $6.5M over six months [13], and insider open-market selling totaled $-272.5K (Form 4). Cerebras is the only named customer, so a delayed build has no offsetting revenue. The filing does not quantify construction cost and discloses that insufficient financing could delay or abandon the AI colocation obligations [19]. Share count rose 207.1 percent in 12 months with a shelf registration on file (reality check).

## Business today
DGXX sells cryptocurrency mining, energy and electricity, colocation services, and Tier III AI data center capacity [0][1]. Revenue was $34.2M and cash was $78.5M as of 2025-12-31 (SEC XBRL). Management says the company is transitioning from Bitcoin mining to AI infrastructure [5].

## Chain position
DGXX occupies the data center operator and developer node, the direct beneficiary of behind-the-meter generation. On-site gas and solar plus storage shorten time to power and bypass utility interconnection queues. Faster deployment increases the leased or used capacity that drives data center revenue.

## Customer graph
Cerebras Systems Inc. is the sole named customer (enterprise, named). Federal award dollars are $0 (USASpending). Two other SEC filers name DGXX (customer graph). Customer evidence is thin: one contract, one counterparty, no government revenue.

## Insider and management signal
Form 4 data show net open-market selling of $-272.5K across 2 buys and 6 sales by 2 insiders, which is weak conviction. Management discloses specific terms: a 10-year term, a fixed take-or-pay fee of $195 per kW per month, phase-specific monthly fees, and defined readiness dates [4][9]. The commercial specificity contrasts with the insider selling.

## Street view
Coverage is effectively absent: unknown analyst count, consensus n/a, mean target n/a (sell-side aggregators). For a $406M market cap name with this contract visibility, thin coverage is itself part of the setup. Any initiation would be a new event, not a revision.

## Non-linear case
Full delivery of the 40 MW Cerebras campus implies roughly $93.6M in annualized colocation revenue, several times the current base [4][7]. For that to compound, Phase 1 must reach ready-for-service by December 15, 2026 and Phase 2 by the end of fiscal Q1 2027 [9], then be replicated at new sites. The precondition is financing, since the filing warns that insufficient funding could curtail the AI colocation obligations [19]. A second named customer would re-rate the equity off contracted backlog.

## Evidence
- Four reporting segments, including AI data centers [0][1].
- AI project assets grew from $11.0M to $59.0M from December 31, 2025 to June 30, 2026 [2].
- Ten-year colocation and master services agreement with Cerebras dated May 4, 2026 [3][6].
- Fixed take-or-pay fee of $195 per kW per month, about $2.925M per month for Phase 1 and $4.875M per month for Phase 2, escalating 3.0 percent annually [4].
- Total deployment of approximately 40 MW at the Columbiana, Alabama campus [7].
- One-time construction payments from Cerebras for both phases [8].
- Phase 1 ready-for-service targeted December 15, 2026; Phase 2 by end of first fiscal quarter of 2027 [9].
- Q2 2026 colocation revenue of $3.4M versus $4.5M in Q2 2025 [10][11].
- Six-month 2026 colocation revenue of $6.5M versus $9.6M in the prior period [13][14].
- Going concern language tied to Tier III initiatives and obtaining significant funding [16].
- Disclosure that insufficient financing may delay, curtail, or abandon AI colocation obligations [19].

## Sizing and survivability
At $33.4M average daily dollar volume (reality check), building a position takes about 8 trading days. Net cash of $78.5M (reality check) supports roughly 12.3 quarters of runway, but build-out costs are not quantified. The 207.1 percent share count increase and shelf registration on file (reality check) are real dilution risks.

## What would change our mind
- A Form 4 with open-market insider buying of meaningful size would counter the current selling signal.
- A second named colocation customer in a 10-Q or 10-K filing would reduce single-customer concentration.
- A federal award to DGXX would open a new customer class beyond the enterprise graph (USASpending).

# DUOT: Managing mobile gas turbines for behind-the-meter power as utility T&D capex flatlines

## Bear case first
DUOT's visible revenue program is an AMA with New APR, and New APR is scaling back scope [9]. The 850 MW is purchased capacity, not a guaranteed fee base; utilization, fee rates, and contract duration are undisclosed [0]. Customers are concentrated in one Fortress-linked program [0][4][5]. Insiders have not bought stock (Form 4), and cash runway is about 0.6 quarters (Reality check). If data center demand grows, DUOT must convert it into expanded AMA scope or new named customers; the filing does not show that.

## Business today
DUOT's Asset Management Services segment generates revenue under an AMA with New APR to manage mobile gas turbines and balance-of-plant inventory [6]. Total revenue was $27.0M and cash was $1.9M at 2025-12-31 (SEC XBRL). Segment revenue is not broken out in the excerpts.

## Chain position
DUOT is not an aeroderivative manufacturer, the first-order beneficiary in the seed map. It sits downstream, managing 850 MW of mobile gas turbines [0]. Fees scale with deployment and operation of behind-the-meter turbines, not with utility T&D capex.

## Customer graph
Named enterprise customers are Fortress, New APR, and Sawgrass [0][4][5]. The filing refers to the counterparty as New APR in [4] and Sawgrass in [5]. Government buyer is Department of Transportation, $2.56M (USASpending); one other filer names DUOT (Customer graph). No data center operator is a named customer, so the data-center link is unproven.

## Insider and management signal
Form 4 shows no open-market insider buying or selling in the trailing 12 months (Form 4). Management names specific counterparties and capacity [0][1], but discloses that New APR is scaling back the AMA [9], so the signal is mixed.

## Street view
No sell-side coverage exists: analyst count unknown, consensus n/a, mean target n/a (Street view). No rating actions are present. Thin coverage is part of the setup.

## Non-linear case
The non-linear path: data center operators need firm power faster than interconnection queues, and Fortress/New APR add more turbines for DUOT to manage. If fees track capacity or utilization, revenue can grow without utility capex. The filing shows a reduction, not an expansion [9], so the path needs a reversal visible in a future 10-Q. Fee structure is undisclosed, so sensitivity is an open question.

## Evidence
- DUOT assisted FIG in purchasing approximately 850 MW, consisting of 30 mobile gas turbine generators and balance-of-plant equipment [0].
- Under the AMA, Duos Energy manages the fleet for New APR [1].
- In December 2024, DUOT entered a series of contracts with Fortress, and a $5.0M cash advance was recognized as revenue in 2025 [4][5].
- The Asset Management Services segment generates revenues through the AMA with New APR [6].
- New APR began to scale back the scope of services under the AMA [9].

## Sizing and survivability
A small fund can build a position in about 24 trading days at $10.5M average daily dollar volume (Reality check). Net cash is $1.9M and runway is about 0.6 quarters (Reality check), so capital or positive cash flow is needed soon. Share count is up 62.1% and a shelf is on file (Reality check), so dilution risk is live.

## What would change our mind
An expanded AMA with higher MW or a new named customer in a 10-Q or 10-K. An open-market insider purchase on Form 4. A federal award naming DUOT as mobile turbine operator (USASpending).

# HYLN: A long-horizon beneficiary at order 3 of utility standby revenue from self-generating data centers, but with no named customers and a two-quarter cash runway.

## Bear case first
The theme describes utility standby revenue, a business Hyliion does not operate. The filings describe the KARNO product line for distributed generation, backup power, and grid balancing, but the theme adds no new segment. The excerpts contain no design wins, ordered backlog, or qualification milestones. The only identifiable revenue is $3.475M (SEC XBRL) against federal awards; no named enterprise customer appears in the excerpts (USASpending). Cash runway is about 2 quarters (Reality check), and a shelf registration adds dilution risk.

## Business today
Hyliion sells the KARNO Power Module, a distributed generator targeting 200 kW to low megawatt applications [3], for backup power [6], grid balancing [7], and microgrids paired with storage and renewables [4][5]. Revenue was $3.475M and cash was $22.938M as of 2025-12-31 (SEC XBRL). Identifiable paying customers are federal agencies (USASpending); no named commercial customers appear in the excerpts.

## Chain position
The company is an order-3 beneficiary with a long horizon. Utilities earn standby and connection fees from self-generating data centers, which makes them more willing to host behind-the-meter generation. Hyliion benefits because data centers need generators like KARNO to self-generate while retaining grid connection, and its placement near load avoids T&D losses [1].

## Customer graph
Government: $22.880M in federal awards, split among DoD $15.641M under N0001424C1305, DOE $6.000M under DEFE0032681, and DoD $0.9999M under N6833525C0397 (USASpending). Enterprise: no named customers in the excerpts, and 0 other filers name the company. Customer evidence is thin; government awards are the only identifiable revenue source.

## Insider and management signal
Trailing 12 months show net open-market insider activity of $0 across 0 buys and 0 sales by 0 insiders (Form 4), which is neutral. Management is specific about KARNO's technical design [0] and target range [3], but gives no quantified orders, capacity targets, or committed capex. The language is descriptive and forward-looking.

## Street view
Sell-side coverage is effectively absent: unknown analyst count, consensus n/a, mean target n/a. No firm rating actions are reported. For a $563M small cap, the absence of coverage is part of the setup.

## Non-linear case
KARNO could move from federal awards to commercial deployments if data center operators or utilities adopt it for backup and grid balancing. The backup power market is well established [6], the grid balancing market is expanding [7], and Resiliency-as-a-Service and Virtual Power Plant models [8] create recurring revenue paths. Success in any one would make revenue a multiple of the $3.475M base (SEC XBRL). What must be true is a named commercial design win and capital to reach manufacturing scale.

## Evidence
- KARNO is distinguished from conventional systems with reciprocating engines or gas turbines [0].
- KARNO is expected to avoid 5% to 10% T&D losses by locating near consumption, versus best-in-class combined cycle plants above 50% efficiency [1].
- Management believes KARNO is an innovative solution in the emerging distributed generation space [2].
- Initial target is 200 kW to low megawatt range [3].
- It integrates with energy storage and renewable sources for hybrid energy solutions [4].
- Paired with storage, solar, or wind, it enables resilient microgrids for EV charging [5].
- The backup power market is well established and positioned to grow [6].
- The grid balancing and servicing market is expanding as utilities seek fast-ramping distributed assets [7].
- Resiliency-as-a-Service and Virtual Power Plant models have emerged to leverage distributed generation [8].
- Lower emissions than internal combustion generators are an opportunity if emissions regulations tighten [9].

## Sizing and survivability
Average daily dollar volume is $25.335M, about 10 trading days to build a position (Reality check). Net cash is $22.358M and cash runway is about 2 quarters (Reality check). Share count is up 1.9% in 12 months and a shelf is on file (Reality check). A small fund can build a position in two weeks, but the cash runway threatens the company before the theme matures.

## What would change our mind
- A 10-Q or 8-K that names a commercial customer or a purchase order for KARNO modules.
- A Form 4 showing open-market insider buying or selling.
- A new or expanded federal award in USASpending beyond the existing DoD and DOE contracts.
- A prospectus supplement indicating a capital raise under the shelf registration.

# NWE: Flat grid capex stalls rate base growth; avoid

## Bear case first
Management guidance contradicts the short directly: 4-6% rate base and EPS growth from a 2024 base of $3.40 EPS and $5.38B rate base [0][1]. The $3.2B capital plan is funded by operations and debt, with equity delayed to 2027 [1][2]. The Black Hills merger adds scale and stability [4]; filings do not mention data center load behind the meter. Dossier signals are mixed: zero insider buying or selling (Form 4), federal customers at $209.2K (USASpending). The short thesis relies on an external grid-capex trend absent from company disclosures.

## Business today
NorthWestern is a fully regulated electric and gas utility; rate base is the primary earnings driver [8]. Coal generation contributes 7-8% of earnings [9]. Revenue was $414.3M and cash $8.8M as of 2025-12-31 (SEC XBRL).

## Chain position
Node: rate-regulated electric utilities (order 1, at-risk, mid horizon). Under cost-of-service regulation, US grid capex flatlining near $180B annually stalls net rate base growth, the main driver of allowed revenue. Management targets 4-6% rate base growth [1], the central tension with the thesis.

## Customer graph
Government: $209.2K in federal awards from Health and Human Services (USASpending). Enterprise: no named customers in the excerpts. Unproven: the data center load that anchors the thesis. Two other filers name the company. Customer evidence is thin: regulated utility margin, not contracted enterprise demand, drives revenue.

## Insider and management signal
Insider conviction is neutral: no open-market buys or sells in 12 months (Form 4). Management is specific and committed: $3.68-$3.83 2026 EPS, 4-6% growth, $3.2B capex plan, 14% FFO/debt, named merger partner [1][2][3][4].

## Street view
Sell-side coverage is unknown: no analyst count, consensus, or mean target available. Thin coverage means the flat-capex scenario is likely unpriced. That coverage gap is part of the setup.

## Non-linear case
If the thesis is correct, utility T&D capex growth stays below 1%, and NorthWestern's 4-6% rate base growth guidance breaks. Equity issuances in 2027 dilute shareholders into a stagnant rate base [2]. The Black Hills merger adds integration risk, and coal generation at 7-8% of earnings [9] becomes a stranded-asset liability as environmental costs rise. The gas revenue requirement steps down with field depletion [6]. The compounding path is a de-rating from growth utility to bond-like multiple.

## Evidence
- 2026 EPS guidance of $3.68-$3.83 affirmed; 4-6% EPS and rate base growth from 2024 base [0][1].
- $3.2B 5-year capital plan, about $300M for South Dakota generation, funded by operations and debt [1].
- Equity issuances expected beginning 2027; FFO/debt target of 14% [2].
- Black Hills merger described as a strategic combination creating scale and stability [3][4].
- NorthWestern is fully regulated; rate base drives earnings [8].
- Coal generation provides about 7-8% of earnings [9].
- Montana gas revenue requirement steps down with natural gas production depletion [6].

## Sizing and survivability
Market cap $4.3B with $33.5M average daily dollar volume, about 8 trading days to build a position (delayed price data). Net cash is -$3.28B against $8.8M cash (SEC XBRL), and equity issuances begin in 2027 [2]; share count is up 0.2% in 12 months (SEC XBRL). The debt load and equity pipeline threaten the thesis if rate base growth stalls.

## What would change our mind
- A Form 4 showing insider open-market buying.
- A 10-K or 8-K filing linking data center load to new T&D investment.
- A federal award or customer contract showing contracted enterprise revenue.

# MEI: Flat US grid capex pushes this electrical equipment supplier toward data center power infrastructure, but the pivot is currently unproven.

## Bear case first
The disconfirming reading is that the data center power infrastructure statement in the 8-K is a general participation claim, not a revenue or order fact [0]. The 10-K sales bridge attributes growth to power distribution products and off-highway lighting, not to data centers [4]. The dossier shows no insider open-market buying (Form 4), no federal awards (USASpending), and no named customers, so the thesis rests on capacity-shift logic rather than visible demand. If utility T&D orders flatten before data center contracts appear, MEI has no offsetting disclosed order flow.

## Business today
Methode sells power distribution products, including busbars, smart connect systems, battery disconnect units, and integrated circuit boards, plus user interfaces, LED lighting, and sensors [1][2]. The 10-K describes these capabilities as a full spectrum of vehicle systems [3], and the sales growth discussion points to commercial vehicle and off-highway markets [4]. As of 2026-05-02, revenue was $1,019.2M and cash was $139.6M (SEC XBRL).

## Chain position
MEI occupies the second-order beneficiary node in the data center buildout: a diversified electrical equipment supplier that can redirect existing switchgear, busway, and transformer capacity to private data center contracts. The economic logic is capacity utilization. Factories need volume to cover fixed costs, so flat utility T&D orders push suppliers toward the faster-growing data center market even at more competitive prices.

## Customer graph
No named enterprise customers appear in the excerpts (unproven). Federal awards are $0 on two Department of Defense contract numbers (USASpending). Three other SEC filers name MEI (SEC XBRL), but the excerpts do not identify them as buyers. Customer evidence is thin and does not validate the data center thesis.

## Insider and management signal
Form 4 records zero open-market insider buys and zero sales in the trailing 12 months (Form 4). Management language is positive, saying MEI has a more focused portfolio, deeper customer relationships, and growing participation in markets including data center power infrastructure [0]. The language is not backed by a named program, committed capex, or a dated milestone.

## Street view
Sell-side aggregators show an unknown analyst count, no consensus, and no mean target (Street view). No firm rating actions can be named from the available data. For a small-cap with no visible sell-side coverage, the absence of coverage is part of the setup.

## Non-linear case
The path to a multiple of today's business is a re-rating from an auto and industrial supplier to a data center power supplier. If MEI converts existing busbar, switchgear, and battery disconnect products into data center electrical room orders, revenue growth could come with limited incremental capital. What has to be true is that utility T&D capex stays flat, data center developers buy private electrical equipment contracts, and MEI wins enough volume to cover fixed costs. The filings do not yet show those design wins or customer commitments.

## Evidence
- The 8-K states a belief that Methode enters the year with a more focused portfolio, a stronger operating model, deeper customer relationships, and growing participation in industrial growth markets, including data center power infrastructure [0].
- The 8-K lists capabilities including power distribution, busbars, smart connect systems, battery disconnect units, integrated circuit boards, user interface components, LED lighting, and sensors [1].
- The 10-K contains the same capability language [2].
- The 10-K says these capabilities form a full spectrum of vehicle systems, from power distribution to user interface components, LED lighting, and sensor applications [3].
- The 10-K attributes an increase to higher sales volumes for power distribution products and higher off-highway lighting volumes, partially offset by lower commercial vehicle lighting volumes [4].

## Sizing and survivability
A small fund can build a position in about 23 trading days at the stated average daily dollar volume of $11.1M (reality check). Net cash is -$185.4M, so debt exceeds cash despite the $139.6M cash balance (reality check). Share count fell 0.6% in the trailing 12 months, so dilution is not a current threat (reality check).

## What would change our mind
An 8-K disclosing a named data center customer, design win, or order backlog would validate the pivot. A 10-K segment note quantifying data center revenue, backlog, or capacity additions would show materiality. A Form 4 open-market purchase by an insider would add conviction where none exists today.

# ESP: Flat utility T&D capex strands a small equipment supplier with no growth catalyst

## Bear case first
The short thesis fails on three protections. ESP holds $18.9M cash against a $9.6M revenue base (SEC XBRL), so flat T&D spending does not create near-term solvency pressure. The $18.7M federal awards (USASpending) are DoD-concentrated but not tied to utility capex, giving a visible revenue floor. The insider selling (Form 4) is negative, but without transaction context it is open evidence, not proof of a broken business. The filing excerpt names no utility customer [0], which leaves the flat-capex link unproven.

## Business today
ESP sells power supplies, power converters, filters, power transformers, magnetic components, power distribution equipment, UPS systems, and antennas [0]. Revenue was $9.6M and cash was $18.9M as of 2025-06-30 (SEC XBRL). The excerpt names products only, not customers or end markets [0].

## Chain position
ESP sits at the transmission and distribution equipment supplier node, first order from utility capex. If utility T&D spending flatlines near $180B, order volume for transformers and distribution equipment stops growing and capacity sits idle. The direct demand link is the mechanism, and ESP has no disclosed offsetting business line [0].

## Customer graph
Visible payers are government: $18.7M in federal awards, all from the Department of Defense, on three vehicles including N6339419C0006 (USASpending). No named enterprise customers appear, and one other filer names the company (USASpending). Federal awards exceed trailing revenue, which is possible because award values are multi-year obligations, not single-period revenue (USASpending) (SEC XBRL). Customer evidence is thin and concentrated, with no observable utility or data-center buyer.

## Insider and management signal
Trailing 12-month open-market activity is a net sell of $1.72M across 134 sales and zero buys (Form 4). The 10-Q contains no management commentary on strategy or growth [0]. Persistent insider selling with no narrative reads as low conviction.

## Street view
No analyst coverage, consensus, or mean target is reported. The absence of sell-side sponsorship is typical for a $189M market cap name, but it also removes any analyst who would need to concede the flat-capex risk. The stock would move on a single filing outcome.

## Non-linear case
The downside path is a margin spiral. Flat utility T&D capex removes order growth, and fixed production costs for transformers and distribution equipment do not adjust quickly [0]. If DoD awards step down at renewal of the three vehicles (USASpending), revenue falls below the $9.6M base. Existing shareholders already absorb 7.1% annual dilution (reality check), and a revenue decline would hit per-share economics from both sides. That turns the $18.9M cash cushion (SEC XBRL) into a slow burn and pushes the $189M valuation down.

## Evidence
- ESP's primary products are power supplies, power converters, filters, power transformers, magnetic components, power distribution equipment, UPS systems, and antennas [0].
- The filed excerpt describes products only and names no customers or end markets [0].
- The 10-Q text contains no management commentary on strategy, capacity, or committed capital [0].

## Sizing and survivability
Average daily dollar volume of $2.9M means a full position takes about 84 trading days (reality check), an illiquidity risk for a small fund. Net cash of $18.9M against $9.6M revenue (SEC XBRL) funds the company for years, so the theme plays out as slow margin erosion, not a cash crisis. The 7.1% share count growth (reality check) helps the short, but a capital raise could reset expectations before the thesis matures.

## What would change our mind
- A 10-Q or 10-K naming a utility or data-center customer with rising backlog.
- A Form 4 with open-market insider buys after 134 sales.
- A new USASpending award from a non-DoD agency diversifying the federal base.

# SLNH: Behind-the-meter solar and storage integrator positioned for data center on-site generation demand

## Bear case first
A disconfirming read starts with the same evidence: one insider sold a net $649.2K over trailing 12 months (Form 4), no named customers appear in the excerpts, and federal awards total only $14.5K (USASpending). The balance sheet shows net cash of -$17.4M and cash runway of about 0.2 quarters (reality check). The behind-the-meter quotes describe the current business, not a new optionality, and the filings do not quantify revenue, market size, or contract pipeline. This is a survival story with an unproven demand thesis.

## Business today
The company builds behind the meter at renewable generation sites, accessing both on-site generation and existing grid interconnection infrastructure [0]. It also builds behind the meter to bypass long interconnection queues and source electricity directly from the generation site [1]. Revenue is $29.7M and cash is $462K (SEC XBRL), but the filing excerpts do not name the buyers.

## Chain position
The company occupies the behind-the-meter solar and storage integrator node. Its stated advantage is avoiding interconnection delays [1] while using existing grid infrastructure to improve power economics [0]. The adoption logic is that data center load growth is met on-site rather than through utility transmission and distribution capex, increasing project volume for integrators.

## Customer graph
Government buyers are small but identifiable: $14.5K in federal awards, including $10.7K from the Department of Veterans Affairs and $3.8K from the Department of Defense (USASpending). Enterprise buyers are unproven: no named customers appear in the excerpts, and one other SEC filer names the company (customer graph). Customer evidence is thin.

## Insider and management signal
Open-market Form 4 activity is net selling of $649.2K across 3 buys and 30 sales by 1 insider over trailing 12 months (Form 4). Management articulates a behind-the-meter strategy with an economic rationale [0][1], but the excerpts show no named programs, capital commitments, or quantified targets.

## Street view
Sell-side aggregator data are absent: analyst count unknown, consensus n/a, mean target n/a (sell-side aggregators). No recent firm rating actions are available. Thin coverage is itself part of the setup.

## Non-linear case
A multiple of today's business requires data center customers to commit to on-site solar and storage projects at scale. That would show up as named contracts in filings and would require flat utility T&D capex to keep grid connection unattractive. With cash runway of about 0.2 quarters (reality check), the company must also fund operations without further dilution. The current evidence does not show that path; it shows a liquidity constraint.

## Evidence
- Building behind the meter at renewable generation sites accesses both on-site generation and existing grid interconnection infrastructure, which management believes can improve power economics and accelerate development timelines [0].
- Building behind the meter bypasses long interconnection queues and sources electricity directly from the generation site [1].

## Sizing and survivability
Average daily dollar volume is $22.2M, so a small fund needs about 12 trading days to build a position (reality check). Net cash is -$17.4M, cash runway is about 0.2 quarters, share count is up 711.4% in 12 months, and a shelf registration is on file (reality check). These facts threaten the thesis.

## What would change our mind
A 10-K or 10-Q naming a data center customer or disclosing backlog or contract value. A Form 4 showing insider open-market purchases after the current selling run. A USASpending federal award material relative to $29.7M revenue.

# ARRY: Avoid, flat grid capex and behind-the-meter margin compression pressure a tracker supplier with no direct revenue path

## Bear case first
The strongest disconfirming read is that ARRY sells equipment, not integration services, so the margin compression theme is indirect. The company states its cost advantage continues to drive adoption across distributed generation and utility-scale markets (filing [2]). No insider has sold stock in the trailing 12 months (Form 4), and the company holds $2.236M in federal awards (USASpending). The expected Q3 2026 closing of a transaction (filing [0]) could add capability. The short thesis requires EPC flow-down clauses (filing [3]) to pass margin cuts to subcontractors, which no filing yet shows, and the filings do not reveal a new business segment or named customers.

## Business today
ARRY sells solar tracking technology and fixed-tilt systems to utility-scale and distributed generation customers who construct, develop, and operate solar PV sites (filing [1][4]). Revenue was $1,284M and cash was $244.4M as of 2025-12-31 (SEC XBRL).

## Chain position
The map position is behind-the-meter integrator margins, order 3, at risk, long horizon. ARRY sits at the equipment supply node upstream of those integrators. As a subcontractor to EPCs, ARRY faces flow-down clauses that tie its obligations to the EPC's end customer terms (filing [3]), making it a pass-through target for pricing pressure.

## Customer graph
Named enterprise customers: none in the excerpts (Customer graph). No other filer names the company (Customer graph). Government: federal awards total $2.236M, all from the Department of Defense: $697.5K, $485.8K, and $416.3K (USASpending). The remaining $1,284M of revenue is unproven, so customer evidence is thin.

## Insider and management signal
Open-market insider activity is zero: 0 buys, 0 sales, 0 insiders (Form 4), which is absent conviction in either direction. Management language is generic, with no named programs or quantified targets tied to the theme (filing [1][3][4]).

## Street view
Sell-side coverage is unknown, with consensus and mean target not available. For a $704M market cap company with no visible analyst ratings, thin coverage is part of the setup: the short thesis is not crowded.

## Non-linear case
The downside compounds if easier financing draws new integrators into behind-the-meter solar and storage for data centers, and they bid away project margins. EPC flow-down clauses (filing [3]) transmit margin compression to ARRY. Utility-scale tracker pricing falls as grid capex flatlines near $180B annually and data center load is met by on-site gas turbines and behind-the-meter solar that never reaches ARRY's utility-scale channel. The $704M market cap would be a multiple lower if revenue stagnates and gross margin compresses. No filing evidence confirms this path, but none refutes it.

## Evidence
- Transaction expected to close in Q3 2026; ARRY describes itself as a global provider of solar tracking technology and fixed-tilt systems to utility-scale and distributed generation customers (filing [0]).
- Business overview repeats the tracker and fixed-tilt provider description (filing [1][4]).
- Cost advantage continues to drive widespread adoption across distributed generation and utility-scale markets (filing [2]).
- EPC flow-down clauses may make subcontractor obligations identical to the EPC's obligations to its end customer (filing [3]).

## Sizing and survivability
A small fund can build a position in about 6 trading days given $44.1M average daily dollar volume (Reality check). The company has net cash of -$183.9M (Reality check), so the balance sheet has little cushion as cash is $244.4M (SEC XBRL). Share count is up 1% in 12 months (Reality check); dilution is mild, but the net debt position adds downside if margins compress.

## What would change our mind
- A Form 4 with open-market insider buying would contradict the zero-conviction insider signal.
- An 8-K disclosing a named behind-the-meter or data center customer contract would show a revenue path tied to the theme.
